name: Southwest Slopes / Standard Scramble
prior_findings: Row is framed as a Class 3-4 scramble; sources say Half Moon has no easy route (easiest line class 5+). Needs re-authoring.

earlier_research.fact: Technical difficulty of the route (scramble vs low-5th/5.6 pitch)
earlier_research.evidence: Two sources agree the peak has no easy route: one says there are at least three difficult and no easy routes to the summit, and an encyclopedia entry rates the easiest route class 5+. That contradicts the header grade 'Class 3-4', overview, pro_needs, hazards and the disciplines=['scrambling'] framing, but no source describes a 'Southwest Slopes/Ridge' line, the 5.6 open-book pitch, or gives a specific YDS grade to adopt. The row's scramble identity appears to be synthesized; it needs a re-author of the whole route (grade, overview, pro_needs, hazards, waypoint 'Class 4 Step', partner requirements), not a minimal patch. Recommend human review; do not publish as a Class 3-4 scramble.

earlier_research.fact: Rope needed for the summit rappel
earlier_research.evidence: The only rappel description found is that parties rappel and down-climb from the summit toward the first tower on the ridge; no source gives the rappel length, anchor, or rope needed. The 100-150 ft figure in descent_text is unsourced, so rope_length_m 30 vs a doubled 60 m cannot be settled. Depends on the unresolved grade question above.

earlier_research.fact: Approach line to the base (over Kangaroo Pass vs talus ramp left of the pass)
earlier_research.evidence: One source describes both lines, but for DIFFERENT routes: the talus gully/ledge angling left from the last soggy meadow to the notch north of Half Moon is the approach for the North Ridge, while the South Face approach continues to Kangaroo Pass and traverses east below Wallaby's south slope to cross the ridge at a low point. Other pages copy that text. No source describes a 'Southwest' route, so which approach belongs to this row cannot be settled until the route itself is identified (see grade finding).

earlier_research.fact: Distance and time from the car to Kangaroo Pass
earlier_research.evidence: Sources disagree: one page puts Kangaroo Pass 3 miles from the hairpin (2 miles to the route fork, 1 more to the pass); a trip report gives 4.4 miles round trip to Wallaby's summit via the pass (implying under ~2 mi to the pass); a hiking guide gives 6.0 miles round trip for Wallaby via the pass; a GPS trip report gives 3.54 mi round trip to the pass. No two agree on one figure, and none give the hiking time.

earlier_research.fact: Hairpin pullout position relative to Washington Pass
earlier_research.correct_value: Hairpin pullout is about 1 mile EAST of Washington Pass (~MP 163); Blue Lake trailhead is on the west side of the pass.
earlier_research.evidence: One source puts the parking at the large hairpin pullout near milepost 163 directly below and east of South Early Winters Spire; a hiking guide says that traveling east, just after the Washington Pass crest the road makes a hairpin turn; a trip report labels it the Highway 20 hairpin turn just east of Washington Pass. The Blue Lake trailhead is reached from the east a little under a mile past the Washington Pass Overlook, i.e. west of the pass, so the hairpin cannot be 0.25 mi east of it.

earlier_research.fact: Summit time within the day
earlier_research.evidence: Internally, summitTimeHrs (10.5) equals totalHrs and the itinerary's return-to-car time, while the itinerary summits at +6.5 hr, so summitTimeHrs holds the car-to-car total. No external source gives a summit time for this line to adopt. Recommend nulling timing.summitTimeHrs (the catalog's established repair for this class) rather than writing a computed number.

earlier_research.fact: Dispersed camping stay limit
earlier_research.evidence: The forest's closure order prohibits camping or occupying a single location for longer than 14 consecutive days (renewed as a 2025 order with the same 14-day limit). A Washington camping guide gives national forest dispersed camping a 14-days-in-30 limit. No 10-day limit found.

earlier_research.fact: Elevation of Kangaroo Pass
earlier_research.evidence: The approach prose says Kangaroo Pass is ~6,800 ft while the Kangaroo Pass waypoint says 6671. A hiking guide states the path reaches Kangaroo Pass at 6671 feet, and a separate trip report labels the pass 6671 on its route. The waypoint is correct; the approach figure is the outlier.

earlier_research.fact: Distance from the hairpin pullout to the Blue Lake trailhead
earlier_research.correct_value: Blue Lake Trailhead is on the west side of Washington Pass, not a quarter mile from the hairpin.
earlier_research.evidence: access.passRequired calls Blue Lake Trailhead 'a quarter mile away' from the hairpin. The Blue Lake trailhead is just under a mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook, and the hairpin is on the east side just after the pass crest, so they are on opposite sides of the pass (their coordinates are ~1.4 mi apart in a straight line).

earlier_research.fact: Rope needed for the summit rappel
earlier_research.evidence: Archived route pages for the peak's documented lines show every one is technical: South Face 5.9+ (or 5.7 A0) Grade III, five pitches; North Ridge 5.7+ Grade III, seven pitches; both recommend double ropes for the rappels and found no fixed anchors. The peak overview says there are at least three difficult and no easy routes. No source describes a southwest scramble, its rappel, anchor or length, so the 100-150 ft figure and the 30 m rope cannot be checked. Would settle: identifying the actual route this row describes (likely none exists as a scramble).

earlier_research.fact: Approach line to the base (over Kangaroo Pass vs talus ramp left of the pass)
earlier_research.evidence: Confirmed on the route pages themselves: the scree gully north of Half Moon from about 2 miles leads to the deep notch that is the base of the North Ridge, while the South Face approach goes over Kangaroo Pass and traverses east below Wallaby to cross the ridge into the basin south of the peak. Each approach belongs to a different documented route and neither page describes a southwest scramble, so which approach this row should carry cannot be settled. Would settle: identifying which documented route this row is.

earlier_research.fact: Distance and time from the car to Kangaroo Pass
earlier_research.evidence: One route page gives Kangaroo Pass as 3 miles from the hairpin; a 2021 hiker's GPS stats give 6.91 miles and 5 hours round trip to the pass (about 3.5 mi one way); another party reports 4.4 miles round trip to Wallaby's summit via the pass, which implies the pass is closer to 2 miles. The straight-line distance from the stored trailhead to the pass pin is about 1.3 mi. Figures range from ~2 to ~3.5 mi one way with no two agreeing, and no source gives a time to the pass. Would settle: a measured track to the pass from the hairpin.

earlier_research.fact: Summit time within the day
earlier_research.evidence: Already resolved: timing.summitTimeHrs is now null in the current row, so it no longer claims the car-to-car 10.5 hr as the summit time.

row.name: Southwest Slopes / Standard Scramble
row.fa: Helmy Beckey, Fred Beckey, and Walt Varney, June 17, 1942 (first ascent of the peak)
hazards: Loose blocks on the upper ridge, especially hazardous to parties below while descending
Lingering snow in the approach gullies and in the shaded notch north of Half Moon into early-mid July
Route-finding on broken, cairn-marked terrain through brush and talus below Kangaroo Pass, easy to lose in poor visibility
Short, low-exposure but unroped Class 4 step just below the summit
row.overview: Half Moon is a crescent-shaped granite fin on the north half of Kangaroo Ridge, between Wallaby Peak (0.23 mi south, the peak's higher neighbor) and Big Kangaroo (8,326 ft) to the north. It sits about two miles east of, and in clear view from, the North Cascades Highway at Washington Pass. The rock is ~45-million-year-old rapakivi-textured granite of the Golden Horn batholith. Fred and Helmy Beckey, with Walt Varney, made the first ascent on June 17, 1942. There is no easy walk-up: at least three technical lines are known (Southwest Ridge, North Ridge, South Face), all involving sustained Class 3-4 scrambling with at least one low-5th-class move. This route takes the Southwest Ridge, generally regarded as the least difficult option, which finishes with a short, low-exposure Class 4 step just below the summit.
row.beta: Half Moon is a SW-to-NE trending rock fin on Kangaroo Ridge between Wallaby Peak and Big Kangaroo, with solid, steep, crack-laden faces. Documented lines include the 1942 first-ascent (original) route, rated roughly Class 5+ (low 5th class) — the easiest known way to the summit — plus at least one modern route, Uncle Wehrly's Toupee (5.10-, trad), and at least 3 other difficult unnamed technical lines. None of these is a non-technical scramble.
row.turnaround: As with other Washington Pass alpine granite objectives, set a turnaround time based on daylight, weather, and party pace rather than a fixed clock time — Cascades crest thunderstorms build in summer afternoons, and the peak's technical routes offer no easy retreat once committed.
row.rock_grade: Class 5+ (an older, unnumbered YDS class rating -- roughly a short, low-5th-class step above scrambling terrain, not a specific numeric grade)
row.face: Kangaroo Ridge, between Wallaby Peak and Big Kangaroo
row.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
row.descent: Reverse the Southwest Ridge. Most parties avoid down-climbing the full lower ridge crest by dropping west into the obvious heather gully toward Early Winters Creek partway down.

waypoints.name: SR-20 Hairpin / Pond Pullout (east of Washington Pass)
waypoints.note: Large paved pullout on Highway 20 just east of Washington Pass, below Liberty Bell/South Early Winter Spire; pick up cairns leading south through brush toward Early Winters Creek.
waypoints.directions: Take Highway 20 to the large hairpin-turn pullout near milepost 163, just east of Washington Pass, at roughly 5,100 ft. It is a big paved pullout sitting below Liberty Bell and South Early Winter Spire, and it doubles as the trailhead for Kangaroo Pass. Park here and start from the east end of the lot, where cairns lead south through the brush toward Early Winters Creek.

waypoints.name: Early Winters Creek Clearing (Airplane Wreckage)
waypoints.note: Small clearing along Early Winters Creek scattered with old wreckage from a small-plane crash; last reliable water before the boot path climbs away from the creek.
waypoints.directions: Drop into the woods from the east end of the pullout and pick up the unsigned but well-used climbers' path. It runs south, staying west of and well above Early Winters Creek; angling down toward the creek itself is the standard route-finding mistake on this stretch. Reaching the clearing at about a mile confirms you are still on line.

waypoints.name: Three-Route Fork below Kangaroo Pass
waypoints.note: Boot path splits toward Half Moon's three route options here; stay on the Southwest Ridge line rather than continuing straight up to the Kangaroo Pass notch.
waypoints.directions: Above the clearing the path climbs through boulder fields and slab benches marked only by intermittent cairns, and the tread all but disappears on the slabs — this is the hardest stretch to follow in fog or fresh snow. It also crosses the toe of the avalanche path that sheds off the col between South Early Winters Spire and Cornice Peak, which is a hazard in early season or after new snow and is better crossed early than once the slope has baked in the sun.

waypoints.name: Kangaroo Pass
waypoints.note: Broad saddle on Kangaroo Ridge shared with approaches to Wallaby Peak and Big Kangaroo; gain the ridge here and traverse toward Half Moon's southwest side.

waypoints.name: Class 4 Step below the Summit
waypoints.note: A short, exposed Class 4 slab step breaks up the otherwise Class 3 Southwest Ridge just below the top; loose blocks reported, test holds before committing.
waypoints.directions: From the pass, contour east below Wallaby's south slopes, staying just under the crest, until you can cross back over the ridge at a low notch north of Half Moon into the basin on its southwest side. That drops you at the foot of the broad southwest gully, which starts as Class 2-3 talus and loose scree where rockfall from any party above you is the real danger. Higher up the gully narrows and steepens onto cleaner rock.

waypoints.name: Half Moon Summit
waypoints.note: Crescent-shaped granite high point of Kangaroo Ridge climbing, first ascended June 17, 1942 by Fred and Helmy Beckey with Walt Varney.

waypoints.name: Heather Gully Descent Cutoff
waypoints.note: Partway down the ridge, cut west off the rock into a steep heather-and-dirt gully dropping directly toward Early Winters Creek; loose footing and easy to lose the boot path in poor visibility.

pro_tips: At the ~2-mile fork below Kangaroo Pass, commit to SW Ridge vs. North Ridge vs. South Face before continuing — they diverge substantially and re-routing costs real time
On descent, cut west into the heather gully partway down the ridge to avoid down-climbing the full lower Southwest Ridge crest

row.pro_needs: Mostly unroped Class 3-4; a short rope and a few small cams/slings are useful for the exposed summit blocks.
row.best_season: Reliable window is mid-summer through early fall (roughly July–September) once snow clears the approach gullies and the shaded notch north of Half Moon, which can hold snow into early-mid July in heavy-snowpack years. Access is also gated by Highway 20's seasonal opening over Washington and Rainy Passes — normally mid/late April through late November or early December, though closures/openings vary year to year (in 2026, winter storm damage delayed the opening to June 14, tying 1974 for the latest season-opening on record).
row.approach: Park at the large Hairpin Turn pullout on Highway 20 near milepost 163 (roughly 5,100 ft), just east of Washington Pass — this doubles as the trailhead for Kangaroo Pass. From the east end of the pullout, drop into the woods and pick up the unsigned but well-used climbers' path (no official trail number; this is the standard Kangaroo Ridge/Wallaby/Half Moon approach). The path runs south, staying west of and well above Early Winters Creek — do not angle down toward the creek itself, a common route-finding mistake. Around 1 mile in you pass a small clearing near the creek where old small-plane wreckage is still visible, a useful landmark that you're on line. Beyond this the path climbs through boulder fields and slab benches with intermittent cairns (route-finding gets genuinely tricky here in fog or fresh snow — the tread all but disappears on the slabs), crossing the toe of the avalanche path that sheds off the col between South Early Winters Spire and Cornice Peak; this slope is a hazard in early-season or after fresh snow and should be crossed with care or avoided later in the day once it's baked in the sun. The path gains the ridge at Kangaroo Pass (~6,670 ft, about 1.5-2 miles and roughly an hour of hiking from the car). From the pass, contour east below Wallaby's south slopes, staying just below the crest, until you can cross over the ridge at a low notch north of Half Moon into the basin on its southwest side — this puts you at the base of the broad southwest gully/slopes that give the route its name. Water is only reliably available near Early Winters Creek in the first mile; carry what you need above the pass. From the base of the gully, the route climbs class 2-3 talus and loose scree — rockfall is a real concern with any party above you — before the gully narrows to a steeper class 4 step of cleaner rock roughly midway up; above that, scrambling leads to a flat belay ledge about 200 ft below the true summit, where the final short technical section begins.
row.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than continuing over the ridge. From the summit, downclimb back to the flat belay ledge about 200 ft below the top; this is where the route's one unavoidable technical bit lives — an open-book crack beside a 60-degree slab (roughly a 60 ft 5.6 pitch on the way up). Most parties do not downclimb this: rappel from slung webbing around a large block on the southwest side of the peak just below the summit to get back down past this section. This is a natural gear/block anchor, not bolted — inspect any existing tat before trusting it and back it up if it looks tired. A single rappel here is on the order of 100-150 ft, so a 60 m rope (doubled) covers it comfortably, and a 30 m single-strand rappel is enough if you stop at the first good ledge/stance; parties differ on exactly where they break it depending on rope length carried, but one rappel is the norm to clear the crux. Below the rappel, continue down the loose class 2-3 southwest gully, taking care with scree and rockfall onto anyone below. Rather than downclimbing the full lower southwest ridge, most parties drop west off the crest partway down into the obvious heather gully, which avoids the worst of the loose rock in the lower gully. From there, cross back over the low notch/ridge point into the basin below Wallaby's south slopes, contour west back to Kangaroo Pass, and descend the climbers' path back through the boulder fields and across the avalanche path to the Hairpin Turn pullout.
row.bail: Retreat is straightforward down the southwest slopes at almost any point.

itinerary.cal: Approach talus is described as best done with snow cover in early spring, or after it melts out by July, since bare talus is exposed and leg-breaking.

days.note: A long roadside day, no camp: from the Hwy 20 Hairpin pullout near Washington Pass, follow cairns/boot path through brush staying above Early Winters Creek toward Kangaroo Pass, then break off into the talus gully/ledge system left of the pass that angles up to the notch north of Half Moon. From the notch, scramble the final rock to the summit fin. Descend by reversing the ridge and dropping into the heather gully back toward Early Winters Creek to avoid down-climbing the full lower ridge crest.

access.fees: None — no climbing permit fee (this is National Forest, not Mount Rainier NP)
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No climbing or wilderness permit required for day climbing. Dispersed camping capped at 14 consecutive days; no camping within ¼ mile of Cutthroat Lake; no campfires at dispersed sites; bear-resistant food storage required; dogs on leash ≤6 ft.
access.closures: Approach is only accessible when SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) is open over Rainy and Washington Passes, roughly mid/late April through late November or early December in a typical year; check WSDOT's mountain pass report before driving, since dates vary and can be delayed by storm damage (as in 2026, when repairs pushed the opening to June 14).
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: No fee is collected at the informal Hairpin Turn highway pullout itself, but carrying a Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful/Interagency pass is recommended — it's required at the developed Blue Lake Trailhead on the west side of Washington Pass.

overnight_permit.where: Nothing to obtain for a night on the climbers' trails. The Early Winters valley campgrounds charge a nightly fee.

road.name: North Cascades Highway (SR 20)
road.status: Open seasonally; closed by WSDOT for winter avalanche/storm risk between roughly late November and mid/late April
road.driveNote: The Hairpin Turn pullout used for the Half Moon approach is at approximately milepost 163, about 1 mile east of Washington Pass, where the highway makes its big switchback below Liberty Bell and the Early Winters Spires.
road.seasonalGate: Winter closure points are typically near the Ross Dam trailhead (MP134) on the west and Silver Star (MP171) on the east, sometimes retreating further to Newhalem (MP120)/Early Winters (MP178) gates in deep winter

climate.fall: Cooling but often stable dry spells continue through September before early-season snow returns.
climate.spring: Snow lingers on the approach into June; the access highway itself often isn't open until mid-to-late April.
climate.summer: Warm and dry; July-August are the most reliable snow-free months for climbing.
climate.winter: Highway closed; deep snow and avalanche terrain make this a non-objective in winter.
climate.typical: High, dry-summer East Cascades alpine climate: warm days with real afternoon thunderstorm potential and cold nights at this elevation; snow can linger in the approach gullies and shaded north notch into early-mid July.

bySeason.fall: Late-season (late Sep–Oct) can bring clear, stable weather but a shorter daylight window and colder nights; an early snowfall can end the season abruptly.
bySeason.summer: Jul-Sep is the reliable weather and snow-free window; check current conditions before early-July attempts.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC maintains a Washington Pass weather station for on-the-ground mountain weather; the area falls within NWS zone WAZ523 (Lower Slopes of the Eastern Washington Cascades Crest) for point forecasts.

emergency.notes: Access depends entirely on SR 20 being open for the season; plan for slow/no cell signal on route and treat a vehicle at the Hairpin Turn pullout as the nearest reliable point to call out from.
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — 24 W Chewuch Rd, Winthrop, WA 98862, (509) 996-4000
emergency.nearestHospital: Mid-Valley Hospital, 810 Jasmine St, Omak, WA — roughly 65 road miles via SR-20 through Winthrop; Three Rivers Hospital in Brewster is a comparable distance. Both are well over an hour's drive, and cell coverage in the Kangaroo Ridge basin is unreliable.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 — Okanogan County Sheriff's Office dispatches; Aero Methow Rescue Service (based in Twisp/Winthrop) provides EMS transport and technical/high-angle rescue for the Methow Valley area in partnership with County Search & Rescue

crowds.estimatePerSeason: unknown - low-traffic; likely well under 20 parties per season

fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light day-climbing pack (helmet, layers, water) - not an overnight-weight approach

approach_variants.name: Hairpin pullout and the ramp to the notch north of Half Moon
approach_variants.notes: Park at the large pullout on the hairpin near milepost 163 and take the unsigned climbers' path south, staying west of and well above Early Winters Creek — angling down toward the creek is the standard error here. Around a mile in, a small clearing near the creek holds the remains of an old light aircraft, a useful confirmation that you are on line. Beyond it the path crosses boulder fields and slab benches with occasional cairns and all but disappears on the slabs. Rather than going right over Kangaroo Pass, cross the last soggy meadow before the trail rears up for the pass and look left: a talus gully, slope and ledge system angles back toward the notch immediately north of Half Moon, and crossing at that notch drops you into the basin on the fin's southwest side.
hazards: The avalanche path shedding off the col between South Early Winters Spire and Cornice Peak
Loose scree and rockfall in the southwest gully with any party above
Cairns and tread vanish on the slab benches in fog or fresh snow
No water above the first mile
approach_variants.baseFinding: HALF MOON IS A FIN, AND THAT IS HOW YOU KNOW YOU ARE UNDER IT. It is a thin, crescent-shaped rock blade trending southwest to northeast, sitting between Wallaby Peak to the south and Big Kangaroo to the north; a broad blocky summit mass with a wide gully splitting it is Wallaby, not this. Aim for the notch immediately NORTH of the fin, gained by the talus ramp that angles back from the meadow below Kangaroo Pass, and cross there into the basin on the southwest side. The route begins at the foot of the broad gully draining that southwest flank. Climb loose class 2-3 talus and scree until the gully pinches down to a short step of noticeably cleaner, more solid rock about halfway up — that step is your confirmation you are in the right gully rather than a neighbouring one. Above it, scrambling reaches a flat belay ledge about 200 ft below the true summit, where the short technical finish starts.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. The pass's elevation is uncertain, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

name: Southwest Slopes (Snow/Scramble)
prior_findings: Breakdown/beta follow the short Swamp Creek south ridge; the rest of the row is the long Rainy Pass / Methow Pass approach. Pick one line or split.

earlier_research.fact: Which line the route describes
earlier_research.evidence: The south-side line from the Swamp Creek pullout (brushy forest, stay climber's right of the ~5,200 ft cliff bands, leave the ridge ~7,200 ft for a notch and summit gully) is the standard short route documented as Mount Hardy's South Face/South Ridge (~4-4.5 mi, ~4,100-4,200 ft); ROUTE BREAKDOWN and beta match it and approach_variants marks it primary. APPROACH, waypoints, itinerary, timing, CLIMBING ROUTE, DESCENT, gain_ft and dist_km instead describe the long Rainy Pass PCT / Methow Pass / southeast-slope approach, which is also a documented way up. Reconciling means choosing one line for the whole row and rewriting many fields (or re-splitting into two routes) — not a minimal patch; left for an owner decision.

earlier_research.fact: Granite Pass elevation
earlier_research.evidence: One trail write-up gives Granite Pass as 6,300 ft; another gives 6,270 ft. Both agree with the camp card (6,300) and put the pass roughly 500 ft below Cutthroat Pass, so the approach's '~6,700 ft' and 'drops slightly' are wrong.

earlier_research.fact: Water at Cutthroat Pass / Porcupine Creek
earlier_research.correct_value: No water at Cutthroat Pass; Porcupine Creek (~mile 2) is the last reliable water, then a dry 7-8 miles over Cutthroat and Granite Passes
earlier_research.evidence: A PCT section description says to fill up at the Porcupine Creek crossing (mile 2) and carry water for at least 7-8 miles, with no water noted at Cutthroat or Granite Pass. A Cutthroat Pass trail guide says there are no water sources at the pass and the Porcupine Creek area is the last good water. The 7-8 miles is the dry stretch onward toward Snowy Lakes, not the ~3 miles up to Cutthroat Pass.

earlier_research.fact: Snowy Lakes side trail: up or down
earlier_research.correct_value: The 0.8-mile side trail climbs (~500 ft) from the PCT to the lakes
earlier_research.evidence: Several trail guides describe the Snowy Lakes spur as climbing: well-graded switchbacks up to Lower then Upper Snowy Lake, a gain of 500+ ft in about half a mile, and 'short and steep' on scree. This agrees with the waypoint elevations and itinerary; the 'descend' wording in two waypoint texts is wrong.

earlier_research.fact: When SR-20 opens
earlier_research.correct_value: SR 20 typically reopens mid/late April to early May and closes late November to mid December
earlier_research.evidence: A regional tourism update relaying the highway's pattern says spring reopening is usually accomplished by early May and avalanches typically close it between late November and mid December. A news explainer says it typically reopens mid-to-late April or early May (recent years April 19-20, 2023 May 10) and shuts in late November or early December. The approach's and trailhead card's 'late May/June through October' is therefore too narrow on both ends, and 'typically just reopened' in June is wrong.

earlier_research.fact: Wilderness permit
earlier_research.correct_value: No overnight or wilderness permit on the Rainy Pass PCT approach; only a parking pass
earlier_research.evidence: One backpacking guide states no overnight permit is needed to camp at Snowy Lakes, only a Northwest Forest Pass for parking; another trip write-up lists only the Northwest Forest Pass. The row's permit, access and camp fields all agree, so the partner skill asking for permit self-issue know-how is the outlier and is removed.

earlier_research.fact: Snowy Lakes turnoff relative to Methow Pass
earlier_research.evidence: The only dissenting field is bivy[1] (the Methow Pass meadow camp card), which places the lakes path about a mile beyond Methow Pass; the waypoints, approach, itinerary and approach variant all put the Snowy Lakes turnoff (about 6,200 ft) before Methow Pass northbound, matching a trip report that reached Methow Pass by returning from the lakes camp. The camp card belongs to the camping clean-up; no patch.

earlier_research.fact: Day-2 elevation from camp to Methow Pass and summit
earlier_research.evidence: The figures are cumulative gain, not net elevation differences: from Upper Snowy Lake (~6,900 ft) the route drops to the PCT turnoff (~6,200 ft) and then climbs ~350-400 ft to Methow Pass, and the off-trail leg undulates, giving ~1,850 ft cumulative for ~1,500 ft net. The same numbers (+350 ft camp to pass, +1,850 ft pass to summit) are recorded in a trip report of this exact itinerary.

earlier_research.fact: Last reliable water
earlier_research.evidence: The only dissenting field is bivy[2].water (Cutthroat Pass camp card, 'roughly three miles'); the waypoint puts Porcupine Creek at mile 2. A PCT hike guide puts the last good water at the Porcupine Creek waterfall/crossing about 2.5 mi up. Camp card owned by the camping clean-up; no patch.

earlier_research.fact: Rainy Pass trailhead parking type
earlier_research.correct_value: Rainy Pass PCT north trailhead is a developed parking lot (short access road, vault toilets) on the north side of SR 20; Swamp Creek is a highway pullout.
earlier_research.evidence: The PCTA trailhead/trip pages describe a short access road on the north side of Highway 20 to a fairly large parking lot with vault toilets, the PCT running through the lot. A separate hike guide describes two pit toilets at the trailhead lot (with overflow cars lining the road in larch season). Only access.permit called it informal shoulder parking.

row.name: Southwest Slopes (Snow/Scramble)
row.fa: Sidney Schmerling and Hermann Ulrichs, 1933 (first recorded ascent of the peak, via this standard southwest line)
hazards: long, mostly off-trail approach via the PCT (Rainy Pass - Cutthroat Pass - Granite Pass - Methow Pass, then cross-country to the peak)
loose scree, talus, and blocky rock on the unmarked upper route, especially near the summit saddle and final gully
lingering snow and possible wet-slide/sluff activity on north-facing terrain and the Swamp Creek route's ~40-degree snow finger into early summer
cliff bands near 5,200 ft on the Swamp Creek approach ridge requiring correct routefinding (stay climber's right)
afternoon thunderstorms and rapid weather changes on the exposed ridge crest and passes
wildfire smoke can reduce visibility and air quality in late summer (Aug-Sept)
SR 20 closes seasonally for avalanche danger, roughly early Dec-Apr/May, cutting off road access to both trailheads entirely
row.overview: Mount Hardy (8,099 ft, or 8,097 ft depending on the survey, within normal survey variance) sits in the Okanogan Range of the North Cascades above the headwaters of the Methow River, just west of Methow Pass on the Pacific Crest Trail and ~1.75 miles southwest of taller neighbor Golden Horn (8,366 ft). It's composed of rapakivi-textured Golden Horn batholith granite (same body as Golden Horn, Tower Mountain and Azurite Peak) and is a prominent, easily-seen summit from SR 20 between Washington and Rainy Passes. Sidney Schmerling and Hermann Ulrichs made the first recorded ascent in 1933; the name was officially adopted in 1973.
row.beta: The standard approach ascends the south ridge via brushy forest to the base of the ridge, then follows the ridge upward while staying climber's right to avoid cliff bands at mid-elevations. From approximately 7,200 feet, leave the ridge and scramble loose scree and granite blocks on the east side to reach a notch below the summit block. From the notch, traverse left and scramble a shallow gully to reach the summit. Snow extends the hiking window and covers loose talus early in the season.
row.turnaround: Given the long approach on the PCT route, set an early-afternoon turnaround for the summit push to avoid the common afternoon thunderstorm window on the exposed ridge and passes.
row.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
row.comms: Cell service is unreliable at the Highway 20 pullout and nonexistent above the forest line. Sat-comm devices (InReach, Spot) recommended for emergencies. Highway 20 is closed seasonally, typically from December through April, depending on snow conditions.
row.descent: Reverse the ascent line: down-climb the scree/talus slopes to the saddle and Methow Pass, then hike out the PCT over Granite and Cutthroat Passes to the Rainy Pass trailhead. Parties using the Swamp Creek line can glissade the upper snow slopes early season when stable, watching for wet-slide/sluff activity on the steep finishing pitch.
obj_haz: residual snow/ice on approach slopes into early summer
remote, long approach with no maintained trail on the final scramble

waypoints.name: Rainy Pass North Trailhead (PCT)
waypoints.note: Large paved lot on the north side of SR 20 at Rainy Pass; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Recreation Pass required for day use.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 20 to Rainy Pass and park in the large paved lot on the north side of the highway. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is needed for day use. The highway sits inside WSDOT's winter closure zone, so access typically runs late April or May through November depending on snowpack.

waypoints.name: Porcupine Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Last reliable, easy water before a long dry 7-8 mile stretch over Cutthroat and Granite Passes — top off here.
waypoints.directions: Head north on the Pacific Crest Trail, climbing steadily through subalpine forest and larch parkland for about 2 miles to the creek. Fill up here, because it is the last easy water before a long dry stretch of switchbacks.

waypoints.name: Cutthroat Pass
waypoints.note: PCT crosses the Skagit/Okanogan county line here; a side trail drops east to Cutthroat Lake while the route continues north on the PCT.
waypoints.directions: Keep climbing north on the PCT for roughly another 3 miles and 1,500 ft of switchbacks to the pass, about 2 to 2.5 hours from the car at a hiking pace. Snow can linger in the north-facing gullies near the pass into early summer.

waypoints.name: Snowfield past Granite Pass
waypoints.note: Trail descends ~700 ft from Cutthroat Pass to this saddle; a steep snowfield just beyond the pass often lingers into August and has caused slide-for-life falls — carry an ice axe early season.
waypoints.directions: Continue north as the trail drops about 700 ft toward the saddle beyond Granite Pass. A steep snowfield just past the pass often lasts into August and has caused slide-for-life falls, so carry an axe if you are here early in the season.

waypoints.name: Snowy Lakes Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the PCT here and climb west on the 0.8-mile Snowy Lakes side trail toward the basin below Tower Mountain and Golden Horn.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the PCT as it contours across open, sparsely treed slopes to Snowy Creek Meadow, a common water and camp stop. The side trail leaves the PCT here.

waypoints.name: Upper Snowy Lake basin
waypoints.note: Established camp on the upper lake ringed by Tower Mountain and Golden Horn; standard base camp for the Hardy climb, treat lake water before drinking.
waypoints.directions: Climb west on the 0.8-mile Snowy Lakes side trail into the basin under Tower Mountain and Golden Horn. Camp on the rocky bench above the upper lake; treat the lake water.

waypoints.name: Methow Pass
waypoints.note: Open plateau at the PCT's crossing of the Cascade Crest just east of Hardy; leave the trail here and head cross-country up the scree/talus benches on Hardy's southeast slope.
waypoints.directions: Drop back down the side trail to Snowy Creek Meadow and rejoin the PCT northbound, then follow it roughly 1 to 1.5 miles and about 350 ft of gain, around an hour, to the open plateau at the pass.

waypoints.name: Mount Hardy summit
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 scramble up sand/scree/talus benches to a saddle then a short south-face rock step to the summit block; views of Golden Horn, Tower Mtn, and the Methow River headwaters.
waypoints.directions: Leave the trail and travel off-trail west and southwest through open heather and talus benches toward the east ridge. Gain the ridge and follow moderate sand, scree and talus, loose in places and with real route-finding, up to the saddle between the true summit and the lower false summit around 7,200 to 7,600 ft. From the saddle several hundred feet of blocky class 2-3 scrambling leads up; a notch below the summit block is crossed before a short, shallow summit gully. Allow roughly 3 hours from the pass.

row.detailed_rack: No ropes or technical climbing gear required for the standard scramble. A climbing helmet is essential for loose rock protection. Microspikes or crampons may be necessary March through May depending on snow conditions; check avalanche forecasts and current condition reports.
what_to_bring: ice axe
crampons (early season)
helmet (loose rock)
map & compass or GPS (extensive off-trail navigation above Methow Pass or on the Swamp Creek ridge)
trekking poles (talus/scree)
layers and a rain shell (afternoon storms)
sun protection for extended above-treeline travel
pro_tips: Camp near Snowy Lakes to break the long PCT approach into two easier days and add a scenic destination in its own right.
The off-trail section from Methow Pass to the summit saddle has no maintained tread; carry a map/compass or GPS since scree benches are easy to misread in flat light.

The Swamp Creek approach (South Ridge/South Face) is a much faster, steeper alternative from a highway pullout ~2 miles west of Rainy Pass for parties comfortable with a sustained ~40-degree snow finish early season.
watch_out: faint/unmarked line off-trail between Methow Pass and the summit saddle — easy to lose in poor visibility
cliff bands force routefinding decisions high on the Swamp Creek ridge
row.pro_needs: Route-finding experience essential; faint boot trail in lower forest and terrain exposure above tree line. The route lacks marked waypoints. Topographic map and compass recommended. GPS and knowledge of scrambling terrain assessment are highly valuable for safe navigation.
row.best_season: Late June through September; July-September gives the driest scree/talus with the least lingering snow. June ascents are feasible but the final slopes/gully still hold snow and require axe/crampons. Regardless of season, the peak is only reachable by car when SR 20 is open (roughly May-November); outside that window the approach becomes a full winter expedition.
row.approach: From the PCT-Northbound (Rainy Pass) trailhead on SR 20 (elev. ~4,855-4,900 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail north. The trail climbs steadily through subalpine forest and larch parkland past Porcupine Creek, reaching Cutthroat Pass (6,820 ft) at about 4.9 miles / ~1,900 ft gain (roughly 2-2.5 hours at a hiking pace). There is no water at the pass itself; Porcupine Creek below is the last reliable source before the high country dries out in late summer, so top off there. From Cutthroat Pass continue north on the PCT, which drops to Granite Pass (~6,300 ft) and then contours across open, sparsely-treed slopes to Snowy Creek Meadow (~6,400-6,900 ft) - a common camp/water stop, with a short side-trail up to Snowy Lakes if you want a higher, more scenic bivy. From the meadow, stay on the PCT northbound roughly another 1-1.5 miles / ~350 ft gain (about an hour) to Methow Pass (~6,600 ft). Leave the trail here: travel west/southwest, off-trail, through open heather and talus benches toward Mount Hardy's east ridge. Gain the ridge and follow moderate slopes of sand, scree and talus - loose in spots, with real route-finding required - up to the saddle between the true summit and a lower false summit (roughly 7,200-7,600 ft). From the saddle, several hundred feet of enjoyable Class 2-3 scrambling over blocky rock leads to the summit at 8,097 ft; some parties note a notch below the true summit block that's crossed before a short, shallow summit gully. Total one-way distance from the trailhead to the summit is roughly 11-12 miles with about 5,100 ft of cumulative gain, matching the recorded figures - this is a long day for strong parties or, more commonly, a 2-day trip with camp near Snowy Creek Meadow/Snowy Lakes. Snow can linger on the upper ridge and in north-facing gullies near Cutthroat and Granite Passes well into early summer; the highway itself (and both this trailhead and the alternate Swamp Creek pullout used for the shorter South Ridge route) sit inside WSDOT's SR 20 winter closure zone, so the route is typically only accessible from around late April or May through November depending on snowpack. Carry an ice axe and know how to use it if attempting before the passes fully melt out.
row.descent_text: Descend the same line used on ascent: reverse the Class 2-3 scramble and scree/talus slopes back down to the saddle, then drop off the east ridge to Methow Pass and rejoin the PCT southbound. Retrace through Snowy Creek Meadow, Granite Pass, and Cutthroat Pass, then back down the PCT to the Rainy Pass trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb - no rappelling is involved on the standard route, so rappels = 0. In early season, lingering snow on the upper south-facing slopes below the saddle can sometimes be glissaded (ice axe and glissading skill required, and only where runouts are clean of rock); by mid-to-late summer this becomes a dry, loose scree/talus descent, so care with route-finding and loose rock is the main hazard, along with the long trail miles back to the car. Some parties returning from camp near Snowy Lakes cut cross-country along the open ridge back toward camp instead of the trail, but parties note this is scenic rather than faster, and it doesn't shorten the standard descent to the trailhead.
row.bail: Retreat is straightforward back down the ascent slopes to Methow Pass (or to the Swamp Creek ridge) — the real hazard is weather/visibility on the exposed ridge and passes, not technical terrain, so turn around early if thunderstorms build.

pitch_detail.notes: Brushy forest with boot trail; 1.2-1.5 miles of elevation gain through mixed conifer forest to ridge base. Faint trail; route-finding experience helpful.
Ridge crest and slabs; stay climber's right to avoid 5,200-foot cliff band. Loose blocks and moderate exposure. Approximately 1,000 feet of elevation gain.
Leave ridge at 7,200 feet, scramble loose scree and granite blocks on east side of ridge toward summit block notch. Loose, steep terrain with exposure. 800+ feet of gain.
pitch_detail.pitch: 3: Scree and Blocks to Summit Block Notch

pitch_detail.notes: Shallow gully scramble from notch to summit. Loose rock, ~100 feet of scrambling to peak. Final exposed section with good granite.

itinerary.cal: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) typically opens for the season in mid-to-late April, but this is a high alpine route that often still holds snow into July, matching the route's 'snow/scramble' character; scree/talus conditions firm up by August-September.

days.note: From the Rainy Pass PCT-northbound trailhead, climb steadily to Cutthroat Pass, then roll over Granite Pass and down into Snowy Creek Meadow before a short side-trail climb to a camp on the rocky bench above Upper Snowy Lake. This is the long approach day; most of the trip's mileage is banked here.

access.fees: None for the climb itself; a Northwest Forest Pass ($5 day / $30 annual) is the standard fee for National Forest trailhead parking in the district.
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No climbing or wilderness permit required for day climbing. Dispersed camping capped at 10 days; no camping within ¼ mile of Cutthroat Lake; no campfires at dispersed sites; bear-resistant food storage required; dogs on leash ≤6 ft.
access.permit: No climbing permit required. There is no fee specific to this off-trail summit route; the Rainy Pass PCT-Northbound trailhead is a developed parking lot with vault toilets, while the Swamp Creek pullout is informal highway-shoulder parking.
access.closures: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) closes for winter between the Ross Dam trailhead (MP 134) and the Silver Star gate (MP 171) — a zone that includes both the Rainy Pass and Swamp Creek trailheads. Typical closure runs early December through April or May depending on avalanche conditions and any DOT repair work; check WSDOT's mountain pass report before planning a trip.
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass recommended for National Forest trailhead parking in this district ($5/day or $30/year); not separately booth-enforced at either pullout.

overnight_permit.where: A Northwest Forest Pass, an America the Beautiful pass, or a Recreation.gov day pass covers parking at the Rainy Pass PCT North trailhead; no permit paperwork is needed to camp anywhere along this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail.

road.name: SR 20 / North Cascades Highway
road.status: Open seasonally only, typically ~May-November; closed by avalanche danger the rest of the year
road.driveNote: Both the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead and the Swamp Creek pullout sit inside the winter closure zone, so the peak is inaccessible by car for roughly half the year.
road.seasonalGate: Gates at Ross Dam (MP 134) and Silver Star (MP 171) close the highway in winter; closure points can move to Newhalem (MP 120) and Early Winters (MP 178) later in the season depending on conditions.

climate.fall: Cooler, often stable weather through September-October before the road closes for winter; early-season snow is possible.
climate.spring: Snow-covered into June; the road may only just have reopened and the upper mountain still holds a continuous snowpack (good glissade conditions but slough/avalanche hazard on warm days).
climate.summer: Typically snow-free by late July/August; the route becomes a dry, loose Class 2-3 talus scramble that is hot and exposed on the south-facing slopes.
climate.winter: Highway 20 is closed for the season; the peak is essentially inaccessible without a very long approach on foot or skis.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate with heavy winter snowfall; summers are drier with clear mornings and a real chance of afternoon thunderstorms/showers, especially July-August.

bySeason.fall: Cools quickly; possible early snow, shorter days, and wildfire smoke can linger into September in bad fire years.
bySeason.spring: Road typically reopens April-May; approach still largely snow-covered — good for early snow climbs but watch for wet-slide activity on steep terrain.
bySeason.summer: Best window (July-Sept); talus/scree mostly snow-free, with real afternoon thunderstorm risk.
bySeason.winter: Highway closed; deep snowpack and avalanche terrain on all approach slopes.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC East Slopes North (Canadian Border to Lake Chelan) for winter/spring avalanche forecasting; check WSDOT's SR 20 pass report for current road status.

emergency.notes: Aero Methow Rescue Service (based in Winthrop/Twisp) provides local EMS and coordinates backcountry evacuations in the Methow Valley. Cell coverage is unreliable to absent along SR 20 and on the peak itself — carry a satellite communicator or PLB.
emergency.county: Okanogan (trailhead side); the summit itself sits on the Okanogan-Skagit county line
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District, 24 W. Chewuch Rd, Winthrop, WA 98862, (509) 996-4000
emergency.nearestHospital: Three Rivers Hospital (Brewster, WA) or Mid-Valley Hospital (Omak, WA) — both roughly 1.5-2 hours' drive from the trailhead via SR 20.

crowds.peakTraffic: Rare even at peak PCT season (July-August); most PCT thru-hikers pass below without detouring to the summit, and there is no maintained trail up the mountain itself
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Very low - roughly 10-20 parties per season, based on the paucity of indexed trip reports

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong, sustained hiking fitness - the PCT approach from Rainy Pass over Methow Pass before even leaving the trail is long, and existing beta flags 'a long return to the trailhead' as a watch-out
fitnessSpec.packWeight: 20-35 lbs; ice axe (and crampons in early season) plus enough food/layers for a full alpine day, heavier if bivying to break up the long approach

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long - a full day of PCT hiking from Rainy Pass over Methow Pass before the scramble portion even begins; many parties treat it as an overnight objective given the round-trip distance
requiredSkills: Self-arrest and steep snow travel with an ice axe (steep snow and cornices early season)
Off-trail routefinding once leaving the PCT near Methow Pass
Weather awareness / turnaround discipline for afternoon thunderstorms
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate to advanced scrambler comfortable with unmarked off-trail routefinding on a remote peak, not a first-scramble objective

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late June through September; July-August is the most dependable stretch, while June still carries meaningful snow

July.reason: Snow retreating on the lower approach; long daylight, though upper mountain snow can linger early in the month

June.reason: SR 20 is normally open, but the upper mountain and approach still hold snow with cornice/steep-snow hazard

August.reason: Best combination of stable weather and minimal snow, matching the climate field's 'best window' summer note

September.reason: Mostly talus/scramble conditions, but shortening days and possible early-season snow late in the month

weather.typical: North Cascades crest-to-east-slope climate; summer is the best window but snow lingers high early on before giving way to talus
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are a real concern in July-August North Cascades high country

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Moderate - loose rock and steep snow/cornice sections carry real fall potential, and the long, remote PCT approach raises the consequence of any injury or benightment

avalanche.zone: Approximate NWAC East Slopes North zone (SR 20/Washington Pass corridor) - not confirmed as a dedicated zone for this exact peak, and NWAC does not issue forecasts during the typical June-Sept climbing season

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass, the crest trail to Methow Pass, and the east ridge
approach_variants.notes: The long way, and the one that suits a two-day trip. From the large paved lot on the north side of SR-20 at Rainy Pass, follow the crest trail north as it climbs steadily through subalpine forest and larch parkland past Porcupine Creek — fill up there, it is the last easy water before a long dry stretch of switchbacks — to Cutthroat Pass. From the pass the trail drops toward Granite Pass and a saddle beyond it, where a steep snowfield often lasts into August and has caused slide-for-life falls, so carry an axe if you are early in the season. Beyond, the trail contours across open, sparsely treed slopes to Snowy Creek Meadow, a common water and camp stop, with a short side trail west into the Snowy Lakes basin for a higher and more scenic bivy under Tower Mountain and Golden Horn. From the meadow, stay on the crest trail north to the open plateau at Methow Pass and leave it there: travel west and southwest off-trail through open heather and talus benches toward the peak's east ridge, gain the ridge, and follow moderate sand, scree and talus — loose in places, with real route-finding — up to the saddle between the true summit and its lower false summit.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September, with July through September giving the driest scree. June ascents work but the final slopes and gully still hold snow and want an axe and crampons. The highway is shut for avalanche control through the winter, which closes both approaches outright.
hazards: loose scree, talus and blocky rock on the unmarked upper route, worst near the summit saddle and the final gully
a steep lingering snowfield just past Granite Pass that has caused slide-for-life falls into August
a long, mostly off-trail final leg with no marked line
afternoon thunderstorms and fast weather changes on exposed ridge crest and passes
wildfire smoke reducing visibility in late summer
seasonal closure of the highway cutting off road access entirely
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE NOTCH IS ON THE FAR SIDE OF THE BLOCK FROM WHERE YOU ARRIVE, AND YOU HAVE TO TRAVERSE TO IT. Whichever approach you used, the climbing starts the same way. At about 7,200 ft the ridge you have been following runs into the summit block; leave the crest there and scramble loose scree and granite blocks across the EAST side — climber's right — until you reach a notch tucked under the summit block. Cross the notch, and the way on is a short, SHALLOW gully leading up to the top. That gully is the marker: it is shallow and blocky rather than deep and cut, and it is the only break that goes at scrambling grade. If the block above you is unbroken wall, keep traversing right rather than starting up; if you have dropped far enough to be under steep cliff bands, you have gone too low and should regain height. The upper ground is several hundred feet of enjoyable blocky scrambling on rock that takes hands, and a lower false summit sits beside the true one — if the highest ground you can reach still has something higher a short distance away, you are on the false summit and the saddle between them is where you crossed.

approach_variants.name: Swamp Creek pullout and the south ridge
approach_variants.notes: The short, steep alternative, and the way most day parties go. Start from the highway pullout at Swamp Creek and climb through brushy forest to the foot of the prominent ridge on the mountain's south side. Follow the ridge upward, staying on the crest where it lets you and moving climber's right to get around the cliff bands that block the crest around 5,200 ft — getting that traverse wrong is what turns parties back. Above the cliff bands the ridge opens out onto sand and scree and continues to the summit block. This side faces the sun and dries early, which is why it comes into condition before the crest-trail approach and why it turns into a loose, dusty grind by late summer; a snow finger on this flank can hold firm snow at a fairly steep angle into early summer, which speeds the ascent considerably for a party carrying an axe.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September once the snow finger has stabilised or melted, with July and August driest. Earlier in the season the finger is a snow climb rather than a scramble.
hazards: cliff bands around 5,200 ft where the crest is blocked and the bypass is on climber's right — the main route-finding failure on this side
a steep snow finger on this flank into early summer, with wet-slide and sluff potential
brushy forest on the lower ridge with no maintained tread
loose scree and blocky rock on the upper route and in the final gully
an exposed ridge crest with no shelter from afternoon thunderstorms
seasonal closure of the highway cutting off road access entirely
