climbing_route.label: East ridge to the saddle
climbing_route.notes: Gain the ridge and follow moderate slopes of sand, scree and talus - loose in spots, with real route-finding required - up to the saddle between the true summit and a lower false summit (roughly 7,200-7,600 ft). Snow can linger on the upper ridge well into early summer; carry an ice axe and know how to use it before the passes fully melt out.

climbing_route.label: Summit scramble from the saddle
climbing_route.notes: From the saddle, several hundred feet of enjoyable scrambling over blocky rock leads to the summit at 8,097 ft; some parties note a notch below the true summit block that's crossed before a short, shallow summit gully.

bivy.name: Rainy Pass PCT north trailhead
bivy.notes: Everything starts from this lot. It is also the start of Whistler Mountain, which is unlike the rest: head east from the parking area into the second gully and follow it to the summit, about four miles round trip and three thousand feet of gain, and no camp helps in the slightest. There is a toilet and no water. Parties routinely sleep in the car here before a long PCT day. As with everything on this stretch of SR 20, access is governed by the winter closure — the highway shuts in late November or early December and normally reopens between mid April and early May, though a bad winter can push it very much later, so confirm before driving. Note also that this specific trailhead has been closed at times for roadwork in recent seasons, which strands the entire zone when it happens.
bivy.water: None at the lot, and this matters more here than it looks. The crest north of the pass is dry, so what you carry out of the car is what you have until well down the far side.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit, no quota and nothing to reserve anywhere in this zone — this is national forest, and the park permit system that governs the country west of here does not apply.
bivy.capacity: A large paved lot on the north-east side of the highway at the pass, shared between climbers, larch-season day hikers and long-distance walkers. It fills early on weekends from late summer onward and there is no overflow.

bivy.name: Methow Pass and the PCT meadow camps below Snowy Lakes
bivy.notes: Methow Pass is where the PCT crosses from the Granite Creek side into the head of the West Fork Methow, and the camps just beyond it are the sheltered alternative to Snowy Lakes for anyone who does not want a night in the open at six thousand seven hundred feet. They cost a little climbing back up on summit morning and are worth it in bad weather. This is also the departure point for Mount Hardy by the long approach: the PCT is left near the pass and a climbers' path leads up toward the peak, which stands directly to the west. Parties combining Hardy with Golden Horn and Tower usually base here or at the lakes and take Hardy on the way out, since the ridge rambling between the lakes and Hardy's south side connects the whole group. Camping on the established sites rather than in fresh meadow matters here more than most places, because the ground is soft and the trail is walked by a steady stream of long-distance hikers all summer.
bivy.water: Good here — this is the drainage side of the crest and the creeks running off toward the West Fork Methow are dependable. It is the reason to choose these camps over the lakes when the wind is up.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping at established sites, no permit and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Rainy Pass.
bivy.capacity: A string of established sites in the meadows along the trail around a mile beyond Methow Pass, near where the boot path to the lakes leaves. Enough ground for several parties spread out, and lower and more sheltered than the lake basin.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Pass, PCT crest camps
bivy.notes: Cutthroat Pass is about five miles north of Rainy Pass by a steadily graded trail and is the first natural stop for anyone heading for Golden Horn or Tower Mountain, though a fit party carrying enough water will push straight past it toward Granite Pass or the lakes. It is not a climbers' camp for any peak — nothing is climbed directly from it — but it is the obvious bad-weather or late-start stop, and it is where a party discovers whether it brought enough water. The larch stands here are the reason the pass is crowded from the third week of September. This is also the point where the Cutthroat Creek trail comes up from the east, so a party can leave one car at each trailhead and walk through.
bivy.water: NONE AT THE PASS, and this is the planning problem of the whole approach. The last certain water is on the climb up, roughly three miles from the trailhead, and there is little to nothing again until close to the lakes far ahead. Carry enough for the evening, the night and the next morning's walk, which for two people is more than most parties expect to shoulder.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit and no reservation. Camp on durable ground rather than in the meadow, and note that the quarter-mile camping closure around Cutthroat Lake, well below and to the east, does not reach up here. Forest-wide campfire bans are normal from mid summer; there is nothing worth burning at this elevation anyway.
bivy.capacity: No established or numbered sites, but a scatter of well-used flat patches on the shoulders and in the larch benches either side of the pass. Several parties can spread out. It is one of the most popular overnight spots on this stretch of trail in larch season, so a Friday arrival in late September will not have it to itself.

bivy.name: Granite Pass
bivy.notes: Granite Pass sits a couple of miles beyond Cutthroat Pass as the trail swings north-west and begins the long traverse under Tower Mountain. Its value is position rather than comfort: it breaks the walk from Rainy Pass to Snowy Lakes into two manageable halves and it puts a party on the right side of the exposed traverse ahead. That traverse is the reason to think about timing — beyond Granite Pass the trail is cut and blasted into the cliffs, and while it is a walk in dry conditions, it is genuinely dangerous under snow. Snowfields cross the trail here into August in a normal year and an axe belongs in the pack until they have gone. Most parties passing through are heading for the lakes and stop here only when the day has run out.
bivy.water: Seasonal at best. There is nothing dependable at the pass and the trail either side of it is dry. Treat this as a dry camp and plan accordingly.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park back at Rainy Pass.
bivy.capacity: One small site at the pass, room for a party or two at most. It is a stopgap rather than a destination and will not absorb a group.

name: West Ridge
prior_findings: name/overview/hazards describe the 2017 West Ridge (to 5.9); most other fields describe the 1961 east ridge. Decide which climb the row is.

earlier_research.fact: Which route the row describes (2017 West Ridge vs standard east ridge)
earlier_research.evidence: The 2017 first-ascent trip report confirms a separate route: the West Ridge ('Bring The Noise'), gained from the crest saddle just east of West Peak and traversed east over the sub-summits Beep and Honk, with belayed climbing to 5.8 and a couple of 5.9 sequences, a double-rope rappel, an unplanned bivy, and a descent by rappel off the summit ridge then the Otto-Himmel gully to Crescent Creek Basin. So the name/overview/hazards describe that route, while rock_grade, pitch_detail, climbing_route, descent, rappels, pro_needs, face and aspect describe the 1961 east ridge (class III per the 1962 AAJ). Only one source documents the West Ridge, and fixing it means rewriting most of the row (and the overview's 'grade not recorded' is itself wrong: the FA report gives up to 5.9) — left open for an owner decision on what this row should be.

earlier_research.fact: Aspect
earlier_research.evidence: The 2017 FA report has the West Ridge approached from the saddle east of West Peak and climbed eastward along the crest to the summit, i.e. a west-facing ridge line not reached from the Otto-Himmel col; aspect S and the face text describe the south-side col approach of the standard route. Depends on the unresolved route-identity question; only one source for the West Ridge.

earlier_research.fact: Side of the col descended
earlier_research.correct_value: The retreat from the col goes back down its south side into Crescent Creek Basin, which can itself be harder late season than the scramble above.
earlier_research.evidence: The 2017 party descended from the Otto-Himmel gully to their Crescent Creek Basin camp via a rappel station above a giant chockstone and face-in snow downclimbing. A traverse party descending south from the col into Crescent Creek Basin in August used three rappel anchors before kicking down the snow finger; the north side leads to the Mustard Glacier. So the retreat is down the south side and it does get harder late season; only the side named in climbing_route was wrong.

earlier_research.fact: Trailhead location
earlier_research.correct_value: 48.6866, -121.2712 (Upper Goodell Creek Group Camp trailhead, ~600 ft)
earlier_research.evidence: Climbing write-ups place the climbers' trailhead at the Upper Goodell Creek Group Campground, reached by following the road uphill from the T-junction, at about 600 ft. USGS 3DEP gives ~611 ft at the pin/approach_logistics coordinate (48.68664, -121.27121) but ~483 ft at the prose coordinate (48.6733, -121.2658), which sits near Goodell Creek's mouth by the lower campground and contradicts the prose's own 'about 600 ft'. The pin, approach_logistics name ('Upper Goodell Group Camp trailhead') and the stated elevation all agree; the prose coordinate is the outlier.

earlier_research.fact: Whether the camp zone permit can be reserved in advance
earlier_research.correct_value: Crescent Creek (and Terror Basin) cross-country zones are walk-up only; not reservable in advance.
earlier_research.evidence: The park's cross-country zones page states that only Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price, Triumph and Tapto Lakes can be reserved in advance and that the remaining cross-country zones (including Terror Basin and Crescent Creek) are walk-up only. The park's backcountry reservations page repeats the same list and says most cross-country zones can only be obtained in person at a permit station. The 60/40 reservable split applies park-wide, not to these zones. The row's own camp cards already say walk-up only.

earlier_research.fact: Rappels on the south side of the Otto-Himmel col
earlier_research.evidence: rappels says none are required on the standard south-side descent, but the 2017 FA party rappelled from a station above a giant chockstone in the Otto-Himmel gully on the way to Crescent Creek Basin, and an August traverse party used three rappel anchors descending the south side of the col. Seasonal snow cover likely decides it; the exact wording of a seasonal rappel note was not settled, so no patch.

earlier_research.fact: Rappels on the south side of the Otto-Himmel col
earlier_research.correct_value: No rappels in early season, when snow fills the gully below the south side of the col; later in the summer the snow melts back and parties rappel the top of the gully (chockstone/moats) from fixed anchors before kicking down the remaining snow.
earlier_research.evidence: A route page for the neighbouring Himmelhorn climb, which uses the same gully from Crescent Creek Basin to the Himmel-Otto col, says the gully is all snow early season but by late season has icy snow, chossy moats and an overhanging boulder near the top, and that descent is trivial early but rap anchors in the moats may be needed late. An August traverse party rappelled from three anchors on the south side of the col before kicking down the snow finger, and the 2017 first-ascent party rappelled from a station above a giant chockstone in the same gully. So 'none required' is only true in early season.

earlier_research.fact: Glacier used on the approach
earlier_research.correct_value: The glacier kit is for the snow and small glacier slopes between Crescent Creek Basin and the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col; the Mustard Glacier lies on the north side and is not part of this route's approach.
earlier_research.evidence: The Mustard Glacier is a small glacier on the northern slope of Himmelhorn, i.e. north of the Otto-Himmel col; a Picket Range overview describes a ramp from the col dropping onto the Mustard Glacier on the far side. The row's own approach, descent_text, bail and rappels all keep the route on the south (Crescent Creek) side and treat the Mustard Glacier as the north-side alternative.

earlier_research.fact: Scramble grade of the standard finish
earlier_research.evidence: The 2003 enchainment party's feature article calls Ottohorn class 3 and one of the few Southern Picket summits that is not fifth class, and a 2011 party also found it 3rd-class scrambling until a fresh rockfall zone forced two 5.7 pitches; the same 2003 party's short report lists the east ridge as class 4. Sources therefore span class 3 to 4, so 'consistently class 3' overstates and a flat 'Class 4' understates; the row's own descent_text (Class 3 with a short Class 4 step) and pro_needs (Class 3-4) already say 3-4.

earlier_research.fact: Round-trip distance
earlier_research.evidence: dist_km renders as the ONE-WAY approach distance; 16.1 km (10 mi) one way is consistent with the 20-mile round trip the approach text quotes for the near-identical Mount Terror approach.

earlier_research.fact: Route identity: 'West Ridge' 2017 line vs an east-ridge description
earlier_research.evidence: The overview and hazards say this is a 2017 west-ridge first-ascent line whose grade, pitch count and length are not recorded, yet rock_grade, pitch_detail, climbing_route, pro_needs and descent_text describe the 1961 standard east ridge from the Otto-Himmel col with grades. The Southeast Route row covers that standard line. Settling it needs an owner decision on whether this row is the 2017 west ridge (and should drop the east-ridge grade/pitch detail) or a duplicate of the standard route; no source describes a 2017 west ridge in detail.

row.name: West Ridge
gear: Ice axe & crampons (snow and small glacier slopes from Crescent Creek Basin to the col)
Glacier travel rope + crevasse-rescue kit (2-3 person rope team)
Light alpine rock rack for the ridge climbing
Helmet (loose rock typical of unrepeated Southern Pickets lines)
hazards: Loose rock, typical of unrepeated Picket Range lines.
Documented by a single 2017 first-ascent trip report — no grade, pitch count, or length is recorded, so treat all difficulty and gear information as unknown.
Deep in the Southern Pickets: a long, committing wilderness approach with route-finding throughout and no realistic prospect of quick outside help.
Afternoon weather deterioration is a recurring hazard on this peak.
row.overview: A 2017 first-ascent line up Ottohorn's west ridge, climbed during the same outing that established two nearby new routes ('Beep' and 'Honk') in the Southern Pickets. Its grade, pitch count and length are not recorded.
row.beta: Established alongside two other new Southern Pickets routes in July 2017; beyond the trip-report title and date, no further route beta (grade, protection, or descent) is publicly available.
row.turnaround: Set a hard turnaround before you leave camp and honour it. Two conditions should stop you regardless of the clock: fresh rockfall debris or visibly unstable blocks on the last 30 ft of the summit ridge (back off and take the north-side variation or go home — one party found exactly this and made the right call), and a moat or bergschrund below the col that has opened enough that you are not confident of recrossing it in the afternoon when it is softer. Weather turnaround: if cloud is filling Crescent Creek Basin, go down while you can still see the Barrier — routefinding across it in a whiteout on loose grassy ledges is how people get hurt here. Because the col is only about an hour from camp, there is almost never a good reason to push a marginal call on this peak.
row.rock_grade: Class 3-4 (a 5.7 variation exists on the north side of the summit blocks)
row.rappels: None on the east ridge, which is normally downclimbed to the col. The south-side gully below the col needs none in early season while snow fills it; later in the summer, as the snow melts back, parties rappel the chockstone and moats at its top from fixed anchors before kicking down the remaining snow. Parties who take the 5.7 variation on the north side of the summit blocks generally make one or two single-rope rappels off slung blocks to regain the ridge. If you continue north out of the col instead of returning to Crescent Creek Basin (i.e. toward the Mustard Glacier and Picket Pass), budget three or more rappels off improvised anchors — a 2011 party built theirs from a driven piton, a slung block and a nut in a constriction, then rappelled the broken couloir and glacier spilling off the north side.
row.face: Crescent Creek Spires — south side, from Crescent Creek Basin via the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn (Otto-Himmel) col
row.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek cross-country zones are walk-up only, issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
row.comms: Assume no cell coverage. The Goodell Creek trailhead sits in a deep valley beside SR 20 near Newhalem with marginal service at best, and there is none on the climbers' path, in Terror Basin or in Crescent Creek Basin. Line-of-sight from high points on the crest occasionally produces a bar or two toward the Skagit valley, but it is not something to plan around. Carry a satellite messenger or PLB — NPS climbing guidance for North Cascades is explicit that parties here must be self-reliant, and a rescue in the Southern Pickets is a multi-day helicopter operation dependent on weather windows. Leave a detailed itinerary with someone at home and file your route with the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount when you pick up the permit.
row.descent: Downclimb the east ridge back to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col, then descend the snow south into Crescent Creek Basin and reverse the approach over the Barrier.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek / Upper Goodell Group Camp trailhead (SR-20, Newhalem)

timing.recommendedStart: From a Crescent Creek Basin camp, leave at first light (roughly 05:00-06:00) so the snow up to the Otto-Himmel col is still firm and the moat crossing is at its most solid, and so you are back at camp with the whole afternoon in hand. A pre-dawn alpine start is not necessary for the climb itself — the col is only about an hour above camp — but it matters if you intend to link Himmelhorn or Mount Terror the same day, or to recross the Barrier and keep descending.

row.detailed_rack: Glacier travel gear for the snow and small glacier slopes from Crescent Creek Basin to the col, plus a light alpine rock rack (assorted nuts + small-to-mid cams ~0.3-2in) and slings for rock steps on the ridge; a 60m rope covers rappelling loose terrain near the Otto-Himmel col.
what_to_bring: North Cascades backcountry permit, picked up in person at Marblemount, since the zones here are walk-up only
Satellite messenger or PLB — there is no cell coverage on any part of this route
Bear canister or a proper hang bag (NPS food-storage rules apply)
Blue bags for human waste on snow and bare rock — never bury it in snow
3-4 L water capacity; the climbers' path has essentially no water for 5,000 ft
GPX or waypoint for the stone arrow at ~1,700 ft where the Terror Creek path leaves the roadbed
Approach shoes for the roadbed plus boots that take crampons
Full storm shell and insulation — maritime squalls hit the Pickets even in August
Sun protection and glacier glasses for the snow basins
Trekking poles for the 5,000 ft climbers' path and the brutal descent of it
Map of the Barrier crossing; it is the single easiest place on the trip to get cliffed out
pro_tips: Camp in Crescent Creek Basin, not Terror Basin. One party reached the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col in about an hour from a Crescent Creek Basin camp — that turns Ottohorn into a short morning instead of a full day with a Barrier crossing at each end.

The turnoff from the Goodell Creek roadbed to the Terror Creek climbers' path is marked only by a stone arrow on the ground at about 1,700 ft, roughly 3.5-4 miles in. Waypoint it before you leave home; people walk past it every season.
Go while there is still snow in the basins. The Otto-Himmel col is straightforward when snow-filled and turns into loose, tricky low-fifth-class rock once it melts out.

Nobody comes all this way for Ottohorn alone. Plan it as one of several summits from a single Crescent Creek Basin camp — Himmelhorn's Wild Hair Crack, Mount Terror and Twin Needles all share the same base.

Treat the last 30 ft as a rockfall zone rather than a scramble. A 2011 party found the standard finish had collapsed into fresh unstable blocks and went around the corner onto two juggy 5.7 pitches instead — the harder line was the safer one that day.
Carry a couple of pitons and be prepared to leave gear. Anchors in this cirque are slung blocks, nuts and driven pins, not fixed stations.
Scout the moat below the col on the way up and remember exactly where you crossed it; it will be softer and wider on the way down.

Pick up the permit and current conditions in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center (360-854-7200) — the rangers there track snow levels on the Terror Creek path and the state of the Barrier.
Build a spare day into the trip. Parties on the Southern Picket traverse routinely burn one to squalls, and both the Barrier and the climbers' path are markedly more dangerous wet.
watch_out: The final ~30 ft to the summit ridge has produced active rockfall; blocks that look welded in place are not.
The south side of the Otto-Himmel col is the friendly side. The north side can demand loose 5th class or rappels once the snow goes, and it commits you to the Mustard Glacier.
Moats and bergschrunds where the snow meets rock below the col open into overhanging pits by late season — one party had to jump one and axe their way out the far side.
The Barrier crossing at about 6,100 ft is 'serious Class 3' on steep, loose, grassy ledges. It is the real crux of the trip and it is not a place to slip.
This is arguably the most isolated terrain in the contiguous United States. A broken ankle in Crescent Creek Basin is a multi-day, weather-dependent helicopter problem.
The Terror Creek climbers' path gains roughly 5,000 ft with almost no water between the creek and treeline — carry it.
Skagit Gneiss in the Pickets swings between excellent and appalling within a single pitch; test everything, and keep the party out of each other's fall line.
row.pro_needs: Protection needs are minimal but the rock quality is the variable. On the standard Class 3-4 east ridge most parties place nothing at all, or slings over blocks and horns for a moving belay through the final step. If the direct summit finish looks loose, the north-side 5.7 variation takes conventional small-to-medium gear in solid, juggy rock and is the safer choice despite the higher grade. The larger protection problem is the snow below the col — a bergschrund and moat that grows through the season — so bring the glacier kit even though the rock rack is trivial.
row.best_season: Mid-July through mid-September is the working window, and earlier in it is generally better. The whole trip is easier with snow: the traverse of Terror Basin, the Barrier crossing and the slopes up to the Otto-Himmel col are all straightforward when snow-filled, and the col specifically is described as easy when snowy and as loose, tricky low-fifth-class rock once melted out. Against that, a big snow year can leave the Terror Basin approach and the climbers' path buried and the basins short of running water in early July. Late July and August are the usual compromise — settled maritime high pressure, the climbers' path melted out, and enough snow left in the basins for travel. By September the col and the moats below it are at their worst, though the summit ridge is at its driest. Outside that window this is a full winter expedition into the most isolated terrain in the lower 48, with an avalanche-prone maritime snowpack.
row.approach: There is no trail to this peak; the approach is the trip. From SR 20 just west of Newhalem, turn north opposite the North Cascades Visitor Center entrance road, go left at the immediate T-junction, past a gravel quarry, then right and uphill on a narrow but well-graded gravel road to the signed Goodell Creek climbers' trailhead (48.6866, -121.2712, about 600 ft). Follow the old roadbed up Goodell Creek for roughly 3.5-4 miles. At about 1,700 ft a stone arrow on the ground marks the unsigned turnoff for the Terror Creek climbers' path — it is easy to walk straight past it, so waypoint it in advance. From the arrow the boot-beaten path climbs relentlessly and steeply up the hillside, gaining about 5,000 ft with essentially no reliable water, to timberline at 5,000-5,200 ft. Above treeline make a rising traverse over meadows, slabs and snowfields toward a 6,200 ft saddle; the standard Terror Basin camp sits about 400 ft below the saddle at roughly 5,800 ft. One party took about 6.5 hours from the trailhead to Terror Basin. For Ottohorn you must keep going west: traverse Terror Basin holding roughly the 6,000 ft contour, then cross the Barrier — the ridge dividing Terror Basin from Crescent Creek Basin — at about 6,100 ft. The Barrier crossing is the non-technical crux of the whole trip: steep, loose, grassy 'serious Class 3' ledges where a slip is not survivable. Drop into Crescent Creek Basin and camp at about 6,200 ft (a good alternative camp sits at 6,400 ft on the Chopping Block ridge overlooking the basin). From that camp, snow and small glacier slopes lead northwest in about an hour to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col at roughly 7,400 ft, where the route proper begins. Note on the numbers: the listed 7,240 ft is the net trailhead-to-summit gain from recorded elevations; the Barrier crossing and the Terror Basin traverse add several hundred feet of extra up-and-down each way, and the near-identical Goodell Creek / Terror Basin / Barrier approach to Mount Terror is recorded at 20 miles and 10,000 ft round trip.
row.descent_text: Reverse the east ridge — 200-250 ft of blocky Class 3 with a short Class 4 step, downclimbed by most parties. If you climbed the 5.7 variation on the north side of the summit blocks, one or two single-rope rappels off slung blocks put you back on the ridge crest; back the anchor up, because the rock here has proven itself capable of moving. From the Otto-Himmel col descend the snow and glacier slopes south back into Crescent Creek Basin. The critical detail here is the moat and bergschrund where the snow meets the rock: it is a non-event when snow-filled in early season and can become an overhanging pit by August. One party descending the equivalent feature on the north side had to jump a large overhanging moat and then climb out the far side with an ice axe. Scout the crossing on the way up and remember where it was; late in the season parties rappel this upper section from fixed anchors. Do NOT descend north out of the col unless you are deliberately continuing toward the Mustard Glacier and Picket Pass — that side takes multiple rappels off improvised anchors down a broken couloir and glacier. From Crescent Creek Basin, recross the Barrier at about 6,100 ft (the steep grassy ledges are considerably worse downhill-facing and tired), traverse Terror Basin at roughly the 6,000 ft contour, then drop the 5,000 ft climbers' path to the stone arrow at 1,700 ft and follow the old roadbed out to Goodell Creek. Give the descent of the climbers' path real respect — it is steep, loose, brushy and hard on knees, and the exit is where most parties are moving slowest.
row.bail: There is no quick exit from Crescent Creek Basin — every retreat goes back over the Barrier into Terror Basin and down the Goodell Creek climbers' path, so plan on a full day out from high camp regardless of what has gone wrong. On the route itself, bailing is easy and cheap: the east ridge can be downclimbed anywhere back to the Otto-Himmel col, and the col is only about an hour of snow above camp. If the summit blocks look freshly loose, retreating from the col and going to Himmelhorn or Terror instead costs nothing. Do not use the north side of the col as an escape — it drops onto the Mustard Glacier and commits you to multiple rappels off improvised gear and, ultimately, to an exit via Picket Pass and the Big Beaver or Access Creek valleys, which is a far bigger undertaking than walking back over the Barrier.

pitch_detail.notes: From camp at roughly 6,200 ft, climb snow and small glacier slopes northwest toward the notch between Ottohorn and Himmelhorn. About an hour from a Crescent Creek Basin camp. Rope up for glacier travel; crampons and axe. Early season this is a straightforward snow plod, late season it becomes bare ice and rubble.
pitch_detail.pitch: Section 1 — Crescent Creek Basin to below the col

pitch_detail.grade: Steep snow, or loose low 5th class late season
pitch_detail.notes: The transition from snow to rock at roughly 7,400 ft. Trivial when snow-filled; by August the moat can be overhanging and the exit onto the col can require loose fifth-class moves. The south (Crescent Creek) side is markedly friendlier than the north. Scout the crossing here for the descent.
pitch_detail.pitch: Section 2 — bergschrund / moat and exit onto the Otto-Himmel col

pitch_detail.notes: From the col, blocky scrambling west up the ridge crest on Skagit Gneiss. Most parties move unroped. Good holds interspersed with detached blocks — keep the party out of each other's fall line.

pitch_detail.grade: Class 3-4 (or 5.7 variation on the north side)
pitch_detail.notes: The final step to the summit at 7,840 ft. Graded Class III by the 1961 first-ascent party and Class 4 by the 2003 enchainment party. In 2011 the direct finish was found to be an active fresh-rockfall zone about 30 ft below the ridge; that party avoided it by moving around the corner onto two juggy 5.7 pitches. Judge it on the day and rope up if there is any doubt.

row.itinerary: Day 1 — Goodell Creek trailhead (600 ft) to Terror Basin camp (5,800 ft), about 6.5 hours; 3.5-4 miles of old roadbed then 5,000 ft of climbers' path. Day 2 — traverse Terror Basin at the 6,000 ft contour, cross the Barrier at about 6,100 ft, and camp in Crescent Creek Basin (6,200 ft) or on the Chopping Block ridge at 6,400 ft; a short day that leaves the afternoon for scouting the line to the col. Day 3 — summit day: about an hour of snow and glacier from camp to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col (7,400 ft), then the east ridge to the summit (7,840 ft) and back to camp; almost everyone links a second objective from the same camp (Himmelhorn's Wild Hair Crack, Mount Terror, or Twin Needles) rather than making a dedicated trip for Ottohorn. Day 4 — recross the Barrier and descend to the trailhead. Build a weather day into the plan: parties on the full traverse routinely lose a day to squalls, and the Barrier and the climbers' path are both much worse wet.

access.fees: Summer backcountry permits cost $10 per person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee; youth 15 and under are free. Fees apply mid-May through early October; permits are free from early October to mid-May. There is no park entrance fee and no parking fee on North Cascades National Park land.
access.permit: A backcountry/wilderness permit is required for every overnight stay, including bivouacs — which means every realistic ascent of this peak. The Terror Basin and Crescent Creek cross-country zones cannot be booked ahead: their permits are walk-up only, issued in person the day of or the day before your trip. The Wilderness Information Center at 7280 Ranger Station Road, Marblemount WA 98267 (360-854-7200) issues permits, lends bear canisters and gives current conditions.
access.closures: No standing closure on this approach. Practical constraints instead: no campfires anywhere in the backcountry zones (stoves only), food must be stored in a bear canister or hung, human waste must be packed out in blue bags on snow and bare rock and never buried in snow or crevasses, and all flagging and webbing left behind counts as trash. Cutting vegetation is illegal and citable. Check with the Wilderness Information Center for temporary closures before each trip.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (National Park Service) — the Southern Picket Range cross-country zone. Trailhead and approach are within the North Cascades National Park Complex.
access.passRequired: No Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is needed to park at the Goodell Creek climbers' trailhead — it is on park land, where NPS charges no entry or parking fee. (Note that many other North Cascades-area trailheads on adjacent Forest Service land do require a Northwest Forest Pass.)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP backcountry permit for the cross-country zone, with a fee
overnight_permit.where: This zone is walk-up only: get the permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, the day of or the day before your trip.

road.name: Goodell Creek Campground access road off SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) at Newhalem
road.status: Open — paved SR 20 to Newhalem, then a short gravel spur past a gravel quarry to a developed climbers' trailhead with parking and a sign noting this is a climbers' trail, not a hikers' trail. Passable to any passenger car.
road.driveNote: From Marblemount follow SR 20 east about 14 miles to Newhalem. Turn north opposite the North Cascades Visitor Center entrance road, go left at the immediate T-junction, continue past a gravel quarry where the pavement ends, then take the right fork uphill on a narrow but well-graded gravel road; the trailhead is on the right within about a mile. Trailhead at 48.6866, -121.2712, roughly 600 ft.
road.seasonalGate: None affecting this approach. SR 20's winter closure gates sit east of Newhalem — the initial closure is between the Ross Dam trailhead (MP 134) and the Silver Star gate (MP 171), moving down to the Newhalem gate (MP 120) and Early Winters (MP 178) in deep winter. Access to Goodell Creek from Marblemount and the west is open year-round.

climate.fall: Early September can be superb: dry rock on the summit ridge, stable air, fewer bugs. The trade-off is that the Otto-Himmel col and the moats below it are at their most melted-out and awkward, and the first Pacific fronts of the autumn arrive without much warning. After late September, storms and short days make the approach and the Barrier crossing dangerous.
climate.spring: Deep, consolidating maritime snowpack. Wet, heavy snow and high avalanche danger on the basins and the couloirs off the crest; cornices along the Southern Picket ridgeline. The Terror Creek climbers' path is usually snow-covered and the approach becomes a serious snow-travel undertaking rather than a hike.
climate.summer: The season. Late July through August brings the most settled high pressure, the climbers' path melts out, and the basins still hold enough snow to make the Terror Basin traverse, the Barrier and the slopes to the col straightforward. Squalls still come through — parties on multi-day traverses routinely lose a day to rain and wind even in August.
climate.winter: Full expedition conditions. Heavy maritime snowfall, high and persistent avalanche danger, and a 5,000 ft approach path buried under snow with no reliable route through the Barrier. Essentially unvisited in winter.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate. Most weather originates over the Pacific and is driven northeast into the Cascades, where orographic lift wrings out heavy precipitation on the western slopes — the Pickets sit right in the firing line. Temperatures are moderated by the maritime influence and rarely drop below 0F or exceed 80F. Expect the range to make its own weather: clear valleys below and cloud sitting on the crest is a normal Picket day.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC 'West Slopes North' avalanche forecast zone.

emergency.notes: Plan as if no outside help is coming quickly. The Picket Range is among the most isolated terrain in the contiguous United States, there is no cell coverage anywhere on the route, and a rescue from Crescent Creek Basin depends on a helicopter and a weather window — realistically a multi-day proposition. Carry a satellite messenger or PLB, leave a detailed itinerary with a contact at home, and register your route with the Wilderness Information Center when collecting the permit. Self-rescue capability (crevasse and moat extraction, improvised rappel anchors, the ability to get an injured partner back over the Barrier) is the practical minimum standard for this trip.
emergency.county: Whatcom County, Washington (the Goodell Creek trailhead and the SR 20 drive are in Whatcom County; the nearest hospital is over the line in Skagit County)
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Road, Marblemount WA 98267 — 360-854-7200. Permits, current conditions, bear canister loans and trip-planning advice.
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth United General Medical Center, 2000 Hospital Drive, Sedro-Woolley WA 98284 — 24/7 Level IV emergency department, ED phone 360-856-6021. It is the critical-access hospital serving Marblemount and the upper Skagit; anything major will be transferred onward.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 for emergencies. Whatcom County Sheriff's Office non-emergency dispatch: 360-676-6911. The WCSO runs search and rescue for the Southern Pickets.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through August, with the Terror Basin path melted out but enough basin snow left to ease the col

July.reason: Early July can still bury the approach, but by late month the path is clear and snow still fills the Otto-Himmel col.

June.reason: The Terror Creek path and basins are buried, avalanche slopes loom over the Barrier traverse, and meltwater is scarce.

August.reason: Settled high pressure, a melted-out climbers' path and enough snow in the basins for fast travel to the col.

October.reason: Early storms and short days on a committing route in the most remote part of the Pickets; walk-up permits end with the season.

September.reason: The summit ridge is driest, but the col melts to loose low-fifth-class rock and the moats below it are at their worst.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Goodell Creek / Upper Goodell Group Camp trailhead (SR-20, Newhalem)

climbing_route.label: Scramble from the Himmelhorn-Ottohorn col
climbing_route.notes: From the col the summit is reported as easy scrambling — most accounts call the peak class 3, with a short class 4 step, and describe it as one of the few Southern Picket summits that is not fifth class. Parties have climbed it from the col in roughly an hour round trip, some without taking rope or rack out of camp. Picket rock is broken and the col itself is loose, so helmets and careful block-testing matter more than the grade suggests; the col is also the retreat point, and getting back down into Crescent Creek Basin late in the season can be harder than the scramble above.

climbing_route.label: Rockfall scar below the summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: At least one party found the easy line broke into a fresh rockfall zone about 30 ft below the summit ridge and backed off rather than cross it, returning with a rope and climbing a roped alternative of about two pitches of juggy 5.7 to the top. Treat this as conditions-dependent rather than fixed: the scar is recent enough that the terrain here may have changed again, and a scramble party arriving without gear may find no acceptable line through the unstable blocks. Carry enough to retreat or to protect a short 5th-class variation, and do not commit to the last 100 ft until you can see it.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

name: South Face
prior_findings: This 'South Face' is Concord Tower's South Face (2 sources).

earlier_research.fact: Which tower and face this route climbs
earlier_research.correct_value: This is Concord Tower's South Face (5.6, 3 pitches, Grade II, FA 1965), starting from the far eastern edge of the Concord-Lexington notch and finishing over the shark fin to Concord's summit. The row is filed on the wrong tower.
earlier_research.evidence: The identical beta (price-of-admission gravelly traverse, sandy spot by the shark fin, pink tricam on the summit block, bolts on the summit, rappel to the notch) and the 1965 Cramer/Anderson/Schuler/Stanley FA are listed under Concord Tower as its South Face; a second route database also lists South Face under Concord Tower with the same FA party and describes the shark fin finish. Settled by research, but the fix is re-filing the row to Concord Tower (area_id, name, summit waypoint), which is out of scope for text patches; patching prose alone would contradict the page's Lexington header.

earlier_research.fact: First ascent
earlier_research.correct_value: Donald Cramer, Donald Anderson, Bruce Schuler, and Fred Stanley, 1965 (the fa field as stored).
earlier_research.evidence: Two independent route databases give the FA as Donald N. Cramer, Donald Anderson, Bruce Schuler and Fred Stanley in 1965. No source found for an Anderson/Scott 1964 ascent. The approach_variants note arguing the FA (and its 'conflicting records' hazard) is removed; fa is unchanged.

row.name: South Face
row.fa: Donald Cramer, Donald Anderson, Bruce Schuler, and Fred Stanley, 1965
hazards: Loose, gravelly rock on the initial traverse pitch
Exposed unroped-feeling scramble sections despite being roped
row.overview: A short, moderate 3-pitch 5.6 up Lexington Tower's south side, starting from the Concord-Lexington notch and finishing over a distinctive rock fin to the true summit.
row.beta: P1 is a gravelly, gently down-sloping traverse to trees, staying right — considered the 'price of admission' pitch. P2 climbs to the ridge crest then becomes a roped hike/scramble to a sandy spot near a feature called the 'shark fin,' with a gear anchor behind a flake. P3, the 'money pitch,' traverses up and over the shark fin and then up the summit block to bolted anchors at the top.
row.turnaround: This is a short route, but the summit-block finish and exposed P2 scramble are still consequential — set a turnaround time appropriate to the day's weather rather than pushing through deteriorating conditions.
row.rappels: From summit bolts: either a single-rope rappel to an intermediate anchor on the face, or a double-rope rappel all the way back to the Concord-Lexington notch.
row.descent: From the summit bolts, either make a single-rope rappel to an intermediate anchor on the face, or a double-rope rappel all the way back down to the Concord-Lexington notch.
obj_haz: Gravelly, down-sloping rock on P1 ("the price of admission pitch")
Roped hike/scramble section on P2 near the "shark fin"

timing.recommendedStart: Morning start; short route but plan around the shared Blue Lake/Liberty Bell approach and afternoon storm risk.

row.detailed_rack: 60m rope; a modest rack with cams in the 0.4-3" range (doubles in finger sizes recommended for confidence), nuts, and a pink tricam for a slot on the summit block. Fixed bolts exist at the summit belay.
what_to_bring: Approach shoes for the notch approach
Helmet for gravelly P1 terrain
pro_tips: Stay right on the gravelly P1 traverse — it's the least protected section of the route.
The pink tricam is specifically useful for a slot on the summit block; don't skip it.
watch_out: P1's down-sloping, gravelly rock has minimal protection
P2 becomes a roped hike/scramble over exposed terrain near the 'shark fin'
Summit block finish on P3 is exposed
row.pro_needs: Light rack overall; the key non-standard piece is a pink tricam for a specific slot on the summit block (P3).
row.best_season: July through September for reliably dry rock; as a south-facing route it can come into condition earlier in the season than the north-facing routes on the tower.
row.approach: Reach the Concord-Lexington notch via the standard Blue Lake Trailhead approach (trending toward the col between Concord and Lexington Towers); the route's first belay starts from the far eastern edge of the notch.
row.descent_text: From the bolted summit anchor, parties either make one single-rope rappel to an intermediate bolted anchor partway down the face and then continue down, or run a full double-rope rappel directly back to the Concord-Lexington notch, from which the standard approach gully/climbers' trail leads back to Blue Lake Trailhead.
row.bail: P1 and P2 offer natural gear-anchor options (flakes/trees) for a rappel retreat back to the notch if needed before committing to the summit block on P3.

access.permit: No climbing permit required; day-use fee only at the formal trailhead.
access.closures: SR-20 closes seasonally for winter; the trailhead is unreachable by car during closure.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful/Interagency Pass at Blue Lake Trailhead.

road.name: North Cascades Highway (SR-20)
road.driveNote: From Winthrop, drive ~31 miles west on SR-20 to Blue Lake Trailhead, just past Washington Pass, for the approach to the Concord-Lexington notch.
road.seasonalGate: Gated for winter roughly mid/late November through mid/late April; check WSDOT mountain pass report before approach.

climate.fall: Good conditions into September/early October before the highway closes for winter.
climate.spring: Highway often still gated by winter snow.
climate.summer: Prime season — south aspect dries out early and holds sun most of the day.
climate.typical: Dry, sunny alpine-rock weather July-September with occasional afternoon convective storms.
climate.forecastZone: NWS zone WAZ048 (Western Chelan County) covers the Washington Pass corridor.

emergency.county: Okanogan County (near the Chelan County line)
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee NF — (509) 996-4000, 24 W Chewuch Rd, Winthrop, WA
emergency.nearestHospital: Mid-Valley Hospital, Omak, WA (509-826-1760) or Three Rivers Hospital, Brewster, WA
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Okanogan County Sheriff/911 Dispatch: 509-422-7232 (non-emergency); dial 911 for emergencies

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September, once the gully to the Concord-Lexington notch is snow-free

July.reason: The south face is dry and the notch gully melts out through the month; long days leave room for the gravelly first-pitch traverse.

June.reason: SR 20 is normally open by now, but snow and ice often fill the gully to the Concord-Lexington notch; an axe and crampons may be needed.

August.reason: Snow-free approach and dry rock; the sunny south face gets hot midday and late-summer wildfire smoke can drift over Washington Pass.

October.reason: The south face stays climbable on clear days, but cold nights, short daylight and early snow before SR 20 closes cut the season off.

September.reason: Cool, stable days suit the sunny south aspect and the approach is dry; larches start turning late in the month.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Concord-Lexington notch, then its FAR EASTERN edge
approach_variants.notes: Reach the Concord-Lexington notch via the standard Blue Lake Trailhead approach, trending toward the col between Concord and Lexington Towers rather than toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully. Higher in that gully a climbers' path appears along its left side and is better than the gully bed. Three pitches.
hazards: Two notches a few hundred feet apart on one ridge
A gully bed better avoided in favour of the path along its left side
Far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col, so fainter tread
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE'S FIRST BELAY STARTS FROM THE FAR EASTERN EDGE OF THE NOTCH. So there are two finds and they nest: the right notch, then the right end of it.

WHICH NOTCH: THE CONCORD-LEXINGTON NOTCH IS THE ONE WHERE CONCORD IS ON ONE SIDE OF YOU AND LEXINGTON ON THE OTHER, AND THE CONCORD WALL IN FRONT OF YOU GIVES ONTO LOW-ANGLE, GRAVELLY LEDGES RATHER THAN A STEEP CRACK SYSTEM. IF YOU ARE FACING A STEEP CRACK SYSTEM, YOU ARE AT THE LIBERTY BELL-CONCORD NOTCH, ONE SADDLE BACK, AND LOOKING AT CONCORD'S NORTH FACE.

WHICH END OF IT: the FAR EASTERN edge. The notch is a gap with two ends; walk to the eastern one before racking up. Concord's south-face routes go the other way, up the wall on the notch's Concord side.

CONFIRM BY HARDWARE, BECAUSE THIS ROUTE HAS A DISTINCTIVE ONE: THERE IS A BOLTED SUMMIT ANCHOR. Parties either make one single-rope rappel to an intermediate bolted anchor partway down the face and continue down, or run a full double-rope rappel directly back to the Concord-Lexington notch. A bolted top and a bolted mid-face station on a three-pitch route is what this line offers.

FROM THE NOTCH THE APPROACH GULLY AND CLIMBERS' TRAIL LEAD BACK TO THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD, which is the same car you started from. That is not true of Lexington's east-side routes, which start at the hairpin pond pullout on the other side of the ridge.

name: East Face
prior_findings: No evidence a 4-pitch 5.6 'East Face' exists on Liberty Bell; the row's own corrections note says its facts came from Lexington Tower. Identity review.

earlier_research.fact: Beta describes a different route
earlier_research.evidence: Outside descriptions of Liberty Bell's East Face list only hard lines (Liberty Crack, Thin Red Line, Freedom Rider etc., 5.10-5.13); the Grade II 5.6 four-pitch line on Liberty Bell is the Beckey Route on the southwest side. row.approach: This is on the East Face, so — like Liberty Crack — the approach is not from the Blue Lake Trailhead but from a separate pullout on SR-20 at the hairpin curve just east of Washington Pass. Park on the north shoulder near the curve, walk back toward the pass to a small pond on the south side of the highway, round its east end, and follow a cairned boot path north into the forest. The path climbs through timber and breaks out onto the talus field directly below the East Face after roughly 20-30 minutes and 0.5 mile (~600-800 ft gain). No water source along the way; watch for the cairned track being hard to follow in low light, and loose talus underfoot at the base.
row.descent_text: Because this is a shorter (4-pitch) line on the East Face rather than a full summit route like Liberty Crack or Thin Red Line, the standard descent is the same notch-based line used across Liberty Bell: downclimb east ~100 ft through trees/loose rock to the 2-bolt station, then one rappel to an intermediate stance followed by a double-rope rappel (or two single-rope raps) into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch — 2 rappels on bolted anchors — then downclimb the scree gully to the climbers' path. Note that because this route (like Liberty Crack) is approached from the East Face pullout rather than Blue Lake Trailhead, returning via the west-side notch means either a car shuttle or a roughly 1-mile roadside walk back to your vehicle; parties who top out near Liberty Crack's finish sometimes instead use that route's dedicated 6-bolt rap line or the 4-double-rope-rap line off M&M Ledge to return directly to the East Face base.
row.bail: Rappel or downclimb to the Beckey descent; retreat is straightforward on this moderate terrain.

approach_variants.name: East Face from the SR-20 hairpin pullout
approach_variants.notes:
Shared with every route on this wall: park at the hairpin turnout on SR-20 just east of Washington Pass, walk back west along the shoulder to the small pond on the south side of the road, round its east end, and follow the cairned boot path north into the trees. It climbs steeply through timber and comes out on the talus directly beneath the East Face in roughly half an hour to an hour.

No water on the way. The cairns are hard to follow in the dark.

If you finish on the true summit and descend the standard west-side notch line you will be about a mile of highway from your car, so plan a shuttle or accept the road walk.

approach_variants.baseFinding: The East Face carries a dense cluster of routes in a short stretch of wall, so identify your line off the big features before you leave the talus rather than by picking the nearest crack. The reference point everybody uses is the large roof high on the left-hand part of the wall — the Lithuanian Lip — which Liberty Crack passes on its right. Anything you start well right of that roof-and-crack system is a different route. Approach ledges at the base are third and fourth class and traverse in from the left, so the start of a line is usually a short sideways walk from where the talus meets the rock, not straight up from it.

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
bivy.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, roughly half a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
